learningObjective: Estimate host-to-device PCIe transfer time and reason about overlap with kernel execution.

canonicalClaims.claim: PCIe transfer time equals size divided by practical bandwidth; when transfer and kernel run in overlapping streams, end-to-end time is max(transfer, kernel), never below the longer of the two.
conditions: Pinned host memory for full PCIe throughput.
Independent streams so H2D DMA and kernel scheduler proceed in parallel.
No dependency between the transfer and the kernel that forces serialization.
nonImplications: Does not imply overlap reduces transfer duration itself; it only hides one behind the other.
Does not imply pageable memory transfers hit the same rate; pageable transfers stage through a driver-managed pinned buffer.

misconceptions.claim: Overlapping cudaMemcpyAsync with a kernel reduces end-to-end time to the shorter of the two.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Overlap gives max, not min. The slower operation still bounds wall time.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: CUDA Best Practices Guide, streams and concurrency

misconceptions.claim: PCIe Gen4 x16 practical H2D bandwidth is 100 GB/s.
misconceptions.whyWrong: PCIe Gen4 x16 theoretical is ~32 GB/s and practical is around 25 GB/s. 100 GB/s corresponds to NVLink or PCIe Gen5 links with multiple aggregated lanes.

misconceptions.claim: Pageable host memory is transferred at the same rate as pinned memory.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Pageable memory is staged through a pinned buffer inside the driver, adding a copy and typically halving throughput.

implementationFacts: PCIe Gen4 x16 theoretical ≈ 32 GB/s; practical ~ 25 GB/s per direction.
performanceScenarios: Deployment pipelines that reload weights via PCIe every batch see PCIe bottlenecks; solutions include keeping weights resident, quantizing to reduce bytes, or NVLink for multi-GPU replication.
